```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(nestedscales)
```

This vignette takes one object apart. The example is a small fuel
classification with every awkward feature: a code reused at two frames, a
frame that cross-cuts another, an atom with no code at one frame, and
attributes stored at three different levels.

```{r fuels}
lt <- data.frame(
  group   = c("Fossil", "Fossil", "Fossil", "Fossil", "Fossil",
              "Bio", "Bio", "Bio", "Power"),
  phase   = c("solid", "solid", "liquid", "liquid", "gas",
              "solid", "liquid", "gas", NA),
  carrier = c("Coal", "Coal", "Oil", "Oil", "Gas",
              "Biomass", "Biomass", "Biomass", "Electricity"),
  fuel    = c("Anthracite", "Lignite", "Diesel", "Gasoline", "NaturalGas",
              "Wood", "Biodiesel", "Biogas", "Electricity")
)
at <- data.frame(
  frame     = c("fuel", "fuel", "carrier", "group", "fuel", "carrier"),
  unit      = c("Anthracite", "Lignite", "Oil", "Bio", "Anthracite", "Gas"),
  attribute = c("lhv", "lhv", "lhv", "lhv", "ef_co2", "ef_co2"),
  kind      = c(rep("property", 4), "factor", "factor"),
  value     = c(26.7, 11.9, 42.5, 15.0, 98300, 56100),
  unit_of_measure = c(rep("GJ/t", 4), "kg/TJ", "kg/TJ"),
  source    = "example"
)
al <- data.frame(
  frame  = c("fuel", "carrier", "fuel", "carrier", "carrier"),
  unit   = c("Anthracite", "Coal", "Electricity", "Electricity", "Electricity"),
  alias  = c("hard coal", "coal", "elc", "elc", "power"),
  source = "example"
)
x <- scale_from_leaftable(
  lt, frames = c("group", "phase", "carrier", "fuel"), key = "fuel",
  attributes = at, aliases = al, name = "fuels"
)
x
```

## The object

A `NestedScale` is an S7 object with seven properties:

```{r props}
S7::prop_names(x)
```

| property | type | holds |
|---|---|---|
| `leaftable` | `data.frame` | one row per atom: one column per frame, the key column, weight columns |
| `frames` | `character` | the hierarchy, ordered coarsest first |
| `members` | named `list` | the ordered code vocabulary at each frame |
| `key` | `character` | the name of the atom column (`"unit"` by default) |
| `meta` | `list` | `name`, `desc`, `weights`, `default_weight`, and whatever the builder adds |
| `attributes` | `data.frame` | values keyed by `(frame, unit)`: `attribute`, `kind`, `value`, `lower`, `upper`, `unit_of_measure`, `source`, `note` |
| `aliases` | `data.frame` | alternative labels keyed by `(frame, unit)`: `alias`, `source` |

Everything else -- parent/child tables, ancestry, shares, resolved
attributes -- is derived on demand; nothing is cached on the object. The
two tables are empty unless the builder fills them; a scale saved by an
earlier version, which had no such properties, loads and validates
unchanged.

## The leaftable

```{r leaftable}
scale_leaftable(x)
```

Each row is one atom. The key column (`fuel` here) is unique and complete.
Frame columns may hold `NA`: `Electricity` has no physical state, so it does
not participate at the `phase` frame, and `na_action=` decides what recasts
do about it. The key may share its name with the finest frame, as here and
in the shipped `carriers`: there the frame column *is* the key column.

## Frames, members, ranks

```{r frames}
scale_frames(x)
scale_atom_level(x)              # the finest frame, or the key
scale_units(x, "carrier")        # the members at one frame
scale_units(x)                   # the atoms
scale_rank(x, "carrier")
```

Codes are **not unique across frames**: `Electricity` is a group and a
carrier here, and `Nuclear`, `Heat`, `Storage`, `Other` are each a group
and a carrier in `carriers`. Every function that takes a code therefore
takes its frame as well.

Navigation is derived from the leaftable and routed through the atoms, so a
frame that cross-cuts another reports overlap rather than invented
containment:

```{r navigate}
scale_nests(x, "carrier", "fuel")    # a tree
scale_nests(x, "phase", "carrier")   # Biomass is solid, liquid and gas
scale_parents(x, "carrier", "Biomass", target = "phase")
scale_ancestors(x, "fuel", "Biogas")
scale_descendants(x, "group", "Fossil")
head(scale_ancestry(x), 4)
```

## The attribute table

Physical attributes live in one long table, and a row may sit on **any**
member, not only on an atom:

```{r attributes}
scale_attributes(x)
```

Reading with a `frame` resolves one value per member, walking to the
nearest coarser frame when a member has none of its own, and says where the
value came from:

```{r resolve}
scale_attributes(x, "lhv", frame = "fuel")[
  c("unit", "value", "unit_of_measure", "origin_frame", "origin_unit")]
```

Attributes are **not weights**. A weight says how big an atom is and drives
aggregation; an attribute is a per-member conversion factor and is consumed
only by `convert_scale()`. The constructor promotes numeric leaftable
columns to weights, so a calorific value must be passed as `attributes=`,
never as a leaftable column. Every attribute name carries a `kind`:
`property` (an invertible ratio) or `factor` (one-way).

```{r kinds}
SCALE_ATTRIBUTE_KINDS
```

`vignette("attributes")` has the reasoning and the full account of
inheritance, sources and conversion.

## The alias table

```{r aliases}
scale_aliases(x)
scale_match(x, c("hard coal", "elc", "Lignite"))
```

One alias may point at several members (`elc` above); matching reports that
as ambiguous unless `frame=` narrows it. Matching is exact and
case-insensitive, with no fuzzy stage.

## Weights and meta

```{r meta}
scale_weights(x)                        # none declared here
S7::prop(x, "meta")[c("name", "desc")]
carriers <- read_scale("carriers")
scale_weights(carriers)
S7::prop(carriers, "meta")[c("name", "source", "palette_version")]
head(S7::prop(carriers, "meta")$labels, 4)
```

`meta$name` is load-bearing: `join_scale()` prefixes the columns it attaches
with `"<name>."`, `scale_map_between()` names its label columns after the
objects, and `write_scale()` needs a name for the definition. The shipped
`carriers` keeps energypal's short and long labels in `meta$labels`; colours
are not stored.

## What the validator guarantees

`scale_from_leaftable()` and every operation that rebuilds a scale enforce:

- the key column is present, unique and complete; every frame is a
  leaftable column and `members` are exactly its non-`NA` values, in a
  stable order;
- weights are numeric and finite;
- every attribute and alias row names a `(frame, unit)` that is a member;
  `value` is finite; `lower <= value <= upper` where given; `kind` is one
  of `SCALE_ATTRIBUTE_KINDS` and one attribute name has one kind;
  `unit_of_measure` and `source` are non-empty; no duplicate
  `(frame, unit, attribute, source)` rows and no duplicate alias rows.

The order of `frames` is a convention, coarsest first; the
direction-dependent rules (`share`, residuals, reconciliation) follow it.

Subsetting keeps the tables consistent: `filter_scale()` and `[` keep the
attribute and alias rows of every surviving member at every frame, and
`prune_scale()` keeps the rows at the frames that survive the collapse.

```{r subset}
fossil <- x["group", "Fossil"]
scale_attributes(fossil)[c("frame", "unit", "attribute", "value")]
```

`prune_scale()` needs the frames above the new atom level to nest, so the
cross-cutting `phase` has to go first:

```{r prune}
tree <- scale_from_leaftable(
  lt[c("group", "carrier", "fuel")], frames = c("group", "carrier", "fuel"),
  key = "fuel", attributes = at, aliases = al, name = "tree"
)
scale_aliases(prune_scale(tree, "carrier"))
```

## Definition files

A scale is stored as a definition, not as an R object: a JSON header with
the three tables inline, or, for large scales, a `<name>.scale/` bundle
directory holding the header and the tables as Arrow IPC or CSV files. The
Python binding reads and writes the same files.

```{r definition}
path <- file.path(tempdir(), "fuels.json")
write_scale(x, path)
cat(head(readLines(path), 12), sep = "\n")
back <- read_scale(path)
identical(scale_frames(back), scale_frames(x))
identical(scale_attributes(back), scale_attributes(x))
```

`write_scale(format = "yaml")` writes the same header as YAML, and
`read_scale()` accepts either. Installed packages register directories of
definitions; `scale_catalog()` lists them and `read_scale(id)` opens one by
its id:

```{r catalog}
scale_catalog()[c("id", "name", "kind", "frames", "n_atoms", "package")]
```

```{r cleanup, include = FALSE}
unlink(path)
```

## The registry

One package-level registry changes behaviour explicitly. **Rules** map
value-column names to their aggregation rule; there is no fallback, and an
unregistered column without `rule=` is an error:

```{r rules}
SCALE_RULES
register_scale_rule("tj", "sum")
register_scale_rule("price", "weighted_mean", weight = "tj")
get_scale_rule("price")
list_scale_rules()
clear_scale_rules()
```

A rule may be scoped to one dimension with `scope=`, so a model's `tj`
column aggregates the same way over fuels, regions and months without
being registered three times -- or differently, when it should.
